basis: fields and palaces of memory
note: Augustine's image of memory as a vast interior storehouse gives a Christian interpretive companion to the commentary's container imagery for what is held, retrieved, or dropped.

basis: searching memory for what has been lost
note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has slipped away; Augustine describes searching memory for a lost item, giving that definition an introspective account.

basis: memory as capacious halls and treasuries
note: The commentary pictures memory as a sequence of containers holding what is entrusted; Augustine describes memory as immense halls containing innumerable images, a close account of memory as a storehouse.

basis: written teaching and unwritten apostolic tradition
note: Basil distinguishes church teaching received from writing from teaching transmitted through unwritten apostolic tradition, a later Christian framework that complicates any simple equation of preserved revelation with pages alone.

basis: Papias prefers the living voice to information from books
note: Papias' reported preference for remembered living testimony over books gives a Christian counter-emphasis: the commentary joins memory to sheets, whereas this reception tradition privileges living recall over written repositories.

basis: Paul delivers what he received, according to Scripture
note: The commentary notes a secondary sense of transmitting a report from another; Paul says he handed on what he had received and frames the message as occurring according to Scripture.

basis: what was received is delivered onward
note: Paul's received-and-delivered formula is a precise early Christian transmission chain for the commentary's sense of passing on a report from another.

basis: each receives wages according to personal labor
note: Paul's reward according to one's own labor closely parallels the commentary's cited content that a person has only what he has striven for.

basis: world passes; the one doing God's will remains
note: The commentary contrasts the preferred worldly life with an afterlife that lasts; John says the world and its desire are passing, while the one who does God's will remains forever.

basis: the world passes; God's doer abides forever
note: The world and its desire pass away while the doer of God's will remains forever, directly matching the contrast of worldly preference and endurance.

basis: the Lord's word endures and is preached
note: The Petrine reuse of the enduring-word formula identifies that lasting word with the gospel preached to its readers, combining permanence and proclamation.

basis: public reading, exhortation, and teaching
note: The triad makes public reading serve exhortation and teaching, placing Christian practice beside the commentary's joined recitation and reminder.

basis: community is a letter written by the Spirit on hearts
note: The commentary joins human retention to written pages; Paul calls the community a letter of Christ written not in ink but by the Spirit on human hearts.

basis: Christ's letter written on hearts
note: Paul contrasts ink and stone with the Spirit's writing on human hearts, a Christian reworking of the commentary's relation between held memory and written sheets.

basis: visible things are temporary, unseen things eternal
note: The commentary contrasts the chosen present life with what endures; Paul distinguishes what is seen and temporary from what is unseen and eternal.

basis: seen things temporary; unseen things eternal
note: The visible-temporary versus invisible-eternal contrast states the same valuation pattern developed around 87:16-17.

basis: each receives what was done in the body
note: Universal appearance before Christ's judgment seat gives the individual recompense setting behind the commentary's sheets-of-Moses-and-Abraham ethics.

basis: stirring readers by way of reminder
note: The commentary says reminder brings a needed matter back to mind; Peter explicitly describes his writing as stirring readers up by reminding them while he is still alive.

basis: recall after the speaker's departure
note: The commentary connects reminder with retrieving what has passed and pages that preserve teaching; Peter writes so his readers can recall these things after his death.

basis: provision for recall after the speaker's departure
note: The author seeks to ensure that readers can recall the teaching after his death, making durable remembrance a stated literary purpose.

basis: remember prophets' words and apostolic command
note: The letter explicitly asks readers to recall former prophetic speech and the apostolic command, joining old writings and present exhortation.

basis: hold teaching received by spoken word or letter
note: The commentary traces recitation into written pages and notes a root sense of transmitted report; Paul tells the community to hold traditions delivered either orally or by letter.

basis: hold traditions taught by word or letter
note: The command explicitly joins oral teaching and written letter as forms of retained tradition, directly comparable to recitation becoming pages.

basis: guard the good deposit entrusted to you
note: The commentary defines forgetting as failing to keep what was entrusted; Paul tells Timothy to guard the entrusted deposit through the Holy Spirit.

basis: guard the good deposit
note: The entrusted teaching is to be guarded through the Holy Spirit, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's definition of forgetting as failing to hold an entrusted thing.

basis: heard teaching entrusted through further teachers
note: What Timothy heard is entrusted to reliable people who will teach others, making preservation a multi-generation oral chain.

basis: Timothy has known sacred writings since childhood
note: The commentary identifies Moses' pages as a source of teaching; Paul points to Timothy's childhood familiarity with sacred writings and their power to make him wise for salvation.

basis: books and especially parchments
note: Paul's request for books and parchments gives a concrete Christian reference for the commentary's material sheets of skin or parchment.

basis: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath from ancient generations
note: James describes Moses as publicly read every Sabbath in city synagogues, a New Testament witness to the continuing recitation of an ancient Mosaic written legacy.

basis: word dwelling richly through teaching and admonition
note: The indwelling word produces reciprocal teaching and admonition, a communal version of 87:9's beneficial reminder.

basis: letters read and exchanged between churches
note: A letter is read in one church and exchanged for reading in another, a concrete case of written teaching being circulated rather than left as an isolated page.

basis: Abrahamic covenant temporally distinguished from later law
note: Paul's argument separates the Abrahamic promise from the law arriving 430 years later, a different ordering of Abraham and Moses that must remain visible beside 87:18-19's paired sheets.

basis: Scripture announces good news beforehand to Abraham
note: The commentary says its message is already in Abraham's and Moses' pages; Paul reads Abraham's promise as Scripture's prior announcement of the gospel to the nations.

basis: Scripture proclaims good news beforehand to Abraham
note: Paul reads the Abrahamic promise as Scripture's advance proclamation of the gospel; it supplies a Christian interpretive analogue, rather than literal Abrahamic pages, for ancient Abrahamic revelation.

basis: command to bear one another's burdens
note: The commentary quotes a rule against one person carrying another's burden; Paul commands mutual burden-bearing, a real ethical counterpoint whose context is helping someone caught in transgression.

basis: each person carries their own load
note: The commentary cites the rule that no bearer carries another's burden; Paul says each person will carry their own load, though his surrounding discussion distinguishes this from helping others in trouble.

basis: each person bears his own load
note: Paul's individual load supplies a direct New Testament comparator to the commentary's cited earlier-sheet claim that no bearer bears another's burden.

basis: Moses values reward above Egypt's treasure
note: The commentary names Moses after rejecting worldly preference; Hebrews says Moses counted reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward.

basis: Moses values future reward above Egypt's wealth
note: Moses judges reproach for the Messiah greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to reward, a particularly apt Mosaic comparison for 87:16-19.

basis: God does not forget faithful work
note: God's refusal to forget service makes divine non-forgetting an ethical and judicial claim beside the commentary's Lord who neither strays nor forgets.

basis: law placed in minds and written on hearts
note: The commentary moves between retained memory and pages; Hebrews quotes a covenant promise that God's laws will be placed in minds and written on hearts.

basis: laws put in minds and written on hearts
note: The new-covenant citation makes divine law both mentally placed and internally written, closely paralleling the commentary's movement from memory to inscription.

basis: hearer looks and then forgets what he was like
note: The commentary warns that a received thing can be let go; James's forgetful hearer leaves the mirror and immediately forgets, making departure from instruction concrete.

basis: forgetful hearer after looking
note: James' hearer immediately forgets after seeing himself, a specific Christian image of received perception that is not retained or acted on.

basis: persevering doer looks into the law and is blessed
note: The commentary links retained remembrance to action; James contrasts the forgetful hearer with one who perseveres in the law and acts, who is blessed.

basis: Spirit teaches and reminds disciples of Jesus' words
note: The commentary joins divine teaching to the promise of not forgetting; Jesus says the Spirit will teach the disciples and remind them of what he said.

basis: Spirit teaches and reminds disciples
note: The Paraclete will teach all things and bring Jesus' words back to memory, directly pairing instruction with divinely secured recollection.

basis: Moses wrote about Jesus
note: The commentary places its present message in Moses' pages; Jesus interprets Moses' writing as testimony about him, a distinct Christian claim about what those pages contain.

basis: Moses wrote of Jesus
note: Jesus' claim that Moses wrote about him is a Christian rereading of Mosaic writing that changes what a reader finds in the pages named in 87:19.

basis: gather leftover fragments so none is lost
note: The commentary pictures forgotten matter as dropped remnants and traces a movement toward gathering; Jesus orders the leftover fragments gathered so that none is lost.

basis: eyewitnesses deliver the word onward
note: Luke begins from traditions delivered by eyewitnesses and servants of the word, a narrative account of report transmission before the written Gospel.

basis: orderly written account compiled from earlier testimony
note: The commentary's q-r-ء discussion presents reading as gathering elements together; Luke says he carefully followed the received accounts and writes them in order.

basis: an orderly written account follows received tradition
note: After the eyewitness delivery described in Luke 1:2, the author writes an orderly account; the verse supplies the distinct written outcome of the oral transmission already in view.

basis: written account meant to establish certainty about teaching
note: The commentary's pages preserve what was recited; Luke states that his account is written so Theophilus can know the certainty of what he was taught.

basis: searching for a lost coin until it is found
note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has slipped away; the woman searches carefully for a lost coin, making recovery an active search rather than passive recall.

basis: ritual meal performed in remembrance
note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord's name immediately before prayer; Jesus tells disciples to repeat a meal in remembrance of him, a distinct Christian liturgical act built around remembrance.

basis: do this in remembrance of me
note: The meal command turns remembrance into a repeated communal act, a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's reminder as an instrument of recall.

basis: Law, Prophets and Psalms written about Jesus' suffering and rising
note: The commentary asserts that its message is found in Abraham's and Moses' pages; Jesus gives a distinct Christian reading in which the wider scriptural corpus points to his passion and resurrection.

basis: Jesus reads Isaiah's scroll in the synagogue
note: The commentary connects recited revelation with prophetic pages; Luke depicts Jesus opening Isaiah's scroll and reading it aloud in a public worship setting.

basis: Jesus says the read scripture is fulfilled that day
note: The commentary says its message was already present in earlier pages; after reading Isaiah, Jesus interprets the passage as fulfilled in the hearers' present.

basis: word taken from the heart before it is believed
note: The commentary contrasts retained reminder with what is lost; in Jesus' explanation of the seed, the devil removes the word from hearers' hearts so they will not believe.

basis: joyful reception without roots ends in falling away
note: The commentary says a reminder benefits the one who retains it; Jesus describes hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away when tested because it has no root.

basis: cares, riches and pleasures choke the word
note: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life; Jesus says worldly cares, wealth and pleasures choke the heard word before it matures.

basis: hearers hold the word fast and bear fruit
note: The commentary says the one who fears remembers; Jesus contrasts good soil that holds the heard word fast and bears fruit with the losses in the preceding soils.

basis: hearers hold the word fast in a good heart
note: In the good-soil explanation, hearers retain the word and bear fruit with endurance, a precise Christian image for held rather than dropped revelation.

basis: Jesus' words will not pass away
note: The contrast of passing heaven and earth with imperishable words is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's passing worldly life and retained divine speech.

basis: gain the world and forfeit one's life
note: Jesus' question about gaining the whole world at the cost of life is a pointed Christian analogue to preferring worldly life over what lasts.

basis: the Father's Spirit speaks through disciples
note: Jesus assures messengers that the Spirit of their Father speaks through them, a New Testament form of divinely enabled prophetic speech.

basis: gain the whole world yet forfeit one's life
note: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life in light of the lasting hereafter; Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world at the cost of one's life.

basis: treasure stored on earth is vulnerable to loss
note: The commentary condemns preferring worldly life to what lasts; Jesus warns against storing treasure where moth and rust consume and thieves break in.

basis: treasure stored in heaven endures
note: The commentary calls the afterlife better and more lasting than worldly life; Jesus contrasts earthly loss with treasure in heaven that is not consumed or stolen.

basis: reader, hearers, and keepers of written prophecy
note: Blessing attaches to the reader, hearers, and those who keep a written prophecy's words, tightly joining book, recitation, hearing, and retention.

basis: John eats a little scroll before receiving a prophetic task
note: The commentary's recitation begins with revelation received by a prophet; John takes a written scroll into himself, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, before being told to prophesy.

basis: take and eat the little scroll
note: John consumes the revealed scroll, a New Testament image of a written message entering the prophet before further speech.

basis: John is told to prophesy again to many peoples
note: The commentary moves received words toward public reminder; after the scroll is eaten, John is commissioned to speak again to many peoples and nations.

basis: must prophesy again after the scroll
note: After the consumed scroll, John is told to prophesy again to peoples and kings; the sequence echoes internalized text becoming renewed proclamation.

basis: books opened; the dead judged by recorded deeds
note: The commentary connects earlier pages with each person's own effort and outcome; Revelation depicts the dead judged from opened books according to their deeds.

basis: dead judged from opened books
note: The opened books of judgment make a Christian image of divine record-keeping beside the commentary's unforgetting Lord and the earlier sheets.

basis: taking away words from prophecy's book
note: The warning against taking away words from the prophetic book gives a Christian textual counterpart to the commentary's insistence that what God gathers is not lost.

basis: remember what was received and heard; keep it
note: The church is commanded to remember received and heard teaching and to keep it, closely mapping receipt, recall, and retention onto 87:6 and 87:9.

basis: name not erased from the book of life
note: The promise not to erase the conqueror's name gives a Christian book-image for being retained before God, alongside the commentary's contrast between forgetting and divine record.

basis: each person gives an account to God
note: The commentary links individual effort with its outcome; Paul says each person will give an account of themselves to God, adding a judgment setting to personal responsibility.

basis: each person gives an account to God
note: Paul's formula of each person giving an account of self directly reinforces the individual accountability the commentary attributes to the earlier sheets.

basis: former writings written for present instruction
note: Paul presents earlier written scripture as instruction for later readers, a Christian account of how first writings remain active in a new community.

basis: Enoch reads heavenly tablets recording human deeds
note: The commentary connects prophetic teaching with preserved pages; Enoch is shown written heavenly tablets and reads a record of human deeds, extending the page motif to a celestial archive.

basis: books of the law torn and burned
note: The persecution's tearing and burning of Torah books provides a historical contrary case to the durable custody imagined by 87:18-19.

basis: Nehemiah founds a library and collects books
note: The account of Nehemiah gathering books about kings, prophets, David, and royal letters gives a rare explicit Jewish image of assembling scattered scriptural materials.

basis: Judas collects books scattered by war
note: Judas' recovery of books dispersed through war closely matches the commentary's path from loss and dispersal to gathered pages.

basis: burned law leaves knowledge inaccessible
note: Ezra laments that the law has been burned and therefore the past and future cannot be known, a direct apocalypse-era opposite to a protected, retained scripture.

basis: Ezra dictates books after the Law has been lost
note: The commentary moves from received recitation to gathered pages; 4 Ezra depicts inspired dictation that restores public books after the earlier Law's loss, making preservation through writing central.

basis: inspired understanding and retained memory
note: After drinking the fiery cup, Ezra's wisdom increases and his spirit retains memory, closely matching divine enablement to remember revelation.

basis: Ezra dictates while five scribes write
note: Five men write what Ezra dictates over forty days, a detailed Jewish scene of inspired speech being gathered into text.

basis: ninety-four books written
note: The completed production of ninety-four books makes collected written revelation, rather than a single remembered saying, the explicit outcome.

basis: book of commandments held fast for life
note: The text calls the law an enduring book and contrasts holding it fast with forsaking it, directly echoing the commentary's held versus lost revelation.

basis: God gives Moses divinely written tablets to teach
note: Jubilees opens by having God give Moses tablets of law and commandment already written for teaching Israel, a Second Temple expansion of the Mosaic written-revelation scene.

basis: Moses is given a written record amid predicted Israelite forgetfulness
note: The commentary links revelation, memory and Moses' pages; Jubilees frames a written account given to Moses as a safeguard in a story that anticipates Israel's disobedience and forgetting.

basis: Moses received and transmitted Torah
note: Its chain from Moses through successive teachers supplies a Jewish model for the commentary's source label on transmitting a report received from another.

basis: plastered cistern that loses not a drop
note: The rabbinic praise of learned retention as a cistern that loses no drop closely realizes the commentary's memory-as-container and dropped-object imagery.

basis: forgetting a word of learning
note: The mishnah treats losing even one learned word as grave, making the commentary's forgetting of an entrusted teaching a concrete Torah-study ethic.

basis: this world as corridor before the world to come
note: The corridor-and-banquet-hall contrast gives a compact rabbinic analogue to preferring the nearer worldly life over the lasting life to come.

basis: forgetting one point of Torah is treated as grave culpability
note: The commentary treats forgetting entrusted teaching as loss; this rabbinic reading of Deuteronomy 4:9 makes forgetting a single learned point a serious covenantal offense.

basis: learning compared to writing on fresh or erased paper
note: The commentary connects remembrance with written pages; this rabbinic saying uses the durability of writing on a clean sheet to explain why learning in youth is more firmly retained.

basis: Mosaic law called the covenant book
note: Ben Sira identifies the law commanded by Moses as the book of the Most High's covenant, a Second Temple way of naming a Mosaic written corpus.

basis: lost law book found and read
note: Hilkiah finds the book of the Torah in the temple and gives it to Shaphan to read, a narrative reversal of scripture left out of use and then recovered.

basis: those written in the book are delivered in the time of distress
note: The commentary joins Moses' pages to the surah's outcomes; Daniel's book records those who will be delivered in a final crisis, linking writing with ultimate fate.

basis: everlasting life and everlasting contempt
note: Daniel's resurrection contrast gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to 87:16-17's preference for the present life over the enduring future.

basis: seal the book until the time of the end
note: Daniel is told to keep the words secret and seal the book until the end; its guarded, delayed access provides a qualified inverse to 87:6's enabled recital and 87:18's available earlier sheets.

basis: court sits and books are opened
note: The heavenly court's opened books give a biblical image for the commentary's Lord whose knowledge of former generations is securely recorded.

basis: Daniel reads the books and understands Jeremiah's years
note: The commentary says the present admonition is already in earlier scriptures; Daniel reads Jeremiah's written prophecy to understand the allotted years, a concrete act of consulting prior pages.

basis: king writes a copy of the Law from the priests' book
note: The commentary connects Moses' pages with a collected written scripture; this law makes the king produce his own copy from the priestly source.

basis: king reads the book all his days to learn fear and obey
note: The commentary says the one who fears will remember; Deuteronomy ties daily reading of the written Law to fear of God and keeping its words.

basis: written Torah read continually to learn fear
note: The king keeps a written Torah with him and reads it all his days in order to fear YHWH and keep its words, concentrating the commentary's book, recitation, retention, and fear motifs in one scene.

basis: words put in a prophet's mouth
note: YHWH puts words in the coming prophet's mouth and requires him to speak them, closely matching the commentary's active causative sense of making a messenger recite.

basis: each person dies for his own sin
note: The legal rule rejects transferring a parent's or child's guilt, directly paralleling the commentary's cited content of Abrahamic and Mosaic sheets that no bearer carries another's burden.

basis: first fruits placed before God with worship
note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord's name before prayer; this liturgy moves from the ancestral recital to presenting the gift and bowing before God.

basis: ancestral deliverance recited in the first-fruits rite
note: The commentary links reminder to scripture and worship; the offerer recites a fixed account of Israel's descent to Egypt and deliverance while presenting first fruits.

basis: word near in mouth and heart
note: The word's nearness in Israel's mouth and heart for doing it gives a compact Torah formulation for revelation that is both recited and inwardly held.

basis: written song taught to Israel as witness
note: The commentary moves from recited revelation to written pages; God tells Moses to write and teach a song so it remains in Israel's mouth as a witness.

basis: write, teach, put the song in mouths
note: Moses must write the song, teach it, and place it in Israel's mouths; it joins written preservation with learned recitation as the commentary does.

basis: song will not be forgotten by descendants
note: The commentary contrasts retained revelation with forgetting; Moses says the taught song will remain in descendants' mouths and testify when later troubles come.

basis: the song will not be forgotten
note: The song's continuing presence in descendants' mouths is explicitly said not to be forgotten, an unusually close scriptural analogue to 87:6.

basis: Moses finishes writing the whole Law in a book
note: The commentary says Moses' pages preserve the message across generations; this verse specifically marks completion of the written book, distinct from its later placement beside the Ark.

basis: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
note: The verse explicitly marks completion of Moses' written Torah, a close biblical comparator for 87:19's named Mosaic sheets.

basis: Book of the Law placed beside the Ark
note: The commentary calls Moses' pages a preserved source for the message; Deuteronomy orders the written Law kept beside the Ark as a standing witness.

basis: place the Torah book beside the ark
note: The finished book is placed beside the ark as a witness, making physical custody part of preserving the words rather than leaving them only to memory.

basis: guard memory; teach children and grandchildren
note: The commentary contrasts preservation with forgetting and commands reminder; Moses warns Israel not to forget what it saw and to pass it to descendants.

basis: words kept on the heart
note: The commentary describes teaching held in memory before it appears on pages; Deuteronomy first places God's words on the heart, the inner counterpart to later visible inscription.

basis: repeating words to children in ordinary daily life
note: The commentary moves from received recitation to remembrance; Moses commands repeated teaching at home, on the road, at bedtime and on rising, embedding words in daily memory.

basis: words written on doorposts and gates
note: The commentary describes written pages as a way to preserve recited teaching; Deuteronomy places the words visibly on household entrances, a distinct public inscriptional form.

basis: forgetting the God who brought Israel out of Egypt
note: The commentary explicitly gives forgetting the secondary sense of abandoning God; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord after receiving his commands, making that sense a covenant warning.

basis: every deed brought into judgment
note: The final judgment of every hidden good or evil deed adds the judicial outcome to the commentary's 53:38-42 sequence of individual burden, effort, and return to God.

basis: spirit returns to God who gave it
note: The return of the spirit to its giver gives a Hebrew Bible formulation beside the commentary's statement that the final endpoint is the Lord.

basis: Hebrew זכרון (zikaron, memorial)
note: The commentary's dhikr family includes remembrance; here the cognate names a written memorial, giving the word-family a concrete inscriptional use.

basis: write as memorial; recite in Joshua's hearing
note: The commentary links reminder to written pages and collected recitation; Exodus commands both a written memorial and oral telling, preserving a past event in two forms.

basis: Hebrew z-k-r / Arabic dh-k-r
note: The Sabbath command uses Hebrew z-k-r, formally cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر, for a liturgical remembering that issues in sanctification.

basis: Moses writes all YHWH's words
note: Moses' writing of all the spoken words supplies a Mosaic instance of divine speech becoming a durable written collection.

basis: Hebrew קרא (qara, read aloud)
note: The commentary's q-r-ء family begins with joining words in recitation; Exodus uses the cognate when Moses reads the written covenant aloud to the people.

basis: Book of the Covenant read to the people
note: The commentary joins recitation to pages; Moses reads a written covenant in the people's hearing, and they answer that they will do its words.

basis: Moses reads the covenant book aloud
note: The written covenant is then read in the people's hearing, giving the read-and-hear sequence behind the commentary's movement from gathered words to pages.

basis: God teaches Moses' mouth
note: God promises to be with Moses' mouth and teach him what to speak, a direct Mosaic counterpart to 87:6's God-caused recitation.

basis: one person's guilt is not borne by another
note: The commentary cites the principle that no burden-bearer carries another's burden; Ezekiel says children do not bear parents' guilt or parents children's, grounding the same individual accountability in a different legal setting.

basis: the sinner bears his own iniquity
note: Ezekiel's sustained individual-accountability claim is a close theological counterpart to the commentary's 53:38 reading of the earlier sheets.

basis: prophet eats a scroll, then must speak its words to Israel
note: The commentary links divine recitation with a prophet's retention; Ezekiel internalizes a written scroll before being sent to transmit its words to the people.

basis: eat the scroll, then speak
note: Ezekiel is commanded to consume the scroll before speaking to Israel, an embodied image of written revelation being internalized and reissued.

basis: scroll fills the belly and tastes sweet
note: The commentary's arc makes written words something received and held; Ezekiel's scroll is taken into his body as nourishment before prophetic speech.

basis: Abraham obeys commands, statutes, and laws
note: Genesis presents Abraham as obedient to divine laws but does not narrate a written Abrahamic corpus; the distinction cautions against simply identifying 87:19's sheets with a Genesis document.

basis: Adam takes and eats the forbidden fruit
note: Genesis depicts Adam's first transgression as eating fruit in the woman's temptation scene rather than naming forgetfulness; it is the necessary biblical counter-narrative to the commentary's Adam of Q 20:115 who forgets and lacks resolve.

basis: Hebrew נשה (nashah, forget), a likely cognate of Arabic نسي
note: The commentary develops Arabic n-s-y as forgetting; Joseph names Manasseh because God made him forget hardship, likely sharing the Semitic root, though this is positive relief from suffering rather than forgetting revelation.

basis: write the vision so a reader can run
note: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader, an explicit practical reason for fixing revelation in readable written form.

basis: forgotten Torah answered by divine forgetting
note: Because the priests have forgotten God's Torah, God says he will forget their children; this directly parallels the commentary's reciprocal forgetting and judgment.

basis: sealed book cannot be read
note: Isaiah's learned reader cannot read the sealed book, a precise inverse scene to 87:6's divine promise to make the messenger recite and retain.

basis: write the oracle on a tablet and in a book as lasting witness
note: The commentary carries recited teaching into preserved pages; Isaiah orders a written record for future time, explicitly making inscription a witness that endures.

basis: write on tablet and book for a future day
note: Isaiah is told to inscribe the testimony so it endures as a witness for the future, a specific biblical reason to preserve prophetic speech in writing.

basis: read the Lord's book; none of the creatures is missing
note: The commentary says collection prevents the recited word from being dropped; Isaiah directs readers to the Lord's book and claims that none of the listed creatures is absent from its account.

basis: seek and read YHWH's book; none missing
note: In the oracle's announced animal assembly, the reader is sent to YHWH's book and told none will be missing because his Spirit has gathered them; that concrete book-and-gathering image sharpens the commentary's claim that what God collects is not dropped.

basis: grass withers but God's word stands forever
note: The contrast between perishing grass and the enduring divine word relates the commentary's passing worldly life to retained and lasting revelation.

basis: God promises not to forget Zion
note: The commentary's promise is that the Prophet will not forget the recited message; Isaiah reverses the direction, portraying God as the one who will not forget Zion even if a mother could forget her child.

basis: God will not forget Zion
note: The maternal comparison culminates in God's refusal to forget Zion, a personal counterpart to the unforgetting Lord and his record in the commentary.

basis: words never depart from mouths
note: The covenant promises that God's words will not depart from the prophet's mouth or his descendants' mouths, a generational form of the no-forgetting promise.

basis: bind testimony and seal Torah among disciples
note: The prophet binds and seals testimony among disciples, coupling guarded writing to a community that carries it forward.

basis: YHWH puts words in Jeremiah's mouth
note: The mouth-touching call scene makes prophetic speech a deposited divine word, illuminating 87:6 before the commentary turns to retention.

basis: prophet finds, eats and delights in God's words
note: The commentary connects recitation with remembering the Lord's name; Jeremiah says he found and ate God's words and that God's name was invoked over him, joining reception of words to prophetic identity.

basis: God gives each according to ways and deeds
note: YHWH's searching judgment and recompense according to each person's ways supplies a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's cited earlier-sheet ethics of personal effort and return.

basis: Israel forgets God despite the bride comparison
note: Jeremiah contrasts a bride who remembers her adornments with Israel that has forgotten God for countless days, making forgetfulness concrete as covenantal abandonment.

basis: God remembers sins no more as an act of forgiveness
note: The commentary cites divine forgetting as abandonment of the unfaithful; Jeremiah uses not remembering sins as covenant forgiveness, giving divine non-remembrance an opposite moral valence.

basis: write spoken prophecies on a scroll
note: YHWH orders Jeremiah to put all the words spoken against Israel and Judah on a scroll, directly joining oral revelation and a written surface.

basis: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the scroll
note: The commentary describes deliberate forgetting and a promise that recited words will not be lost; the king deliberately destroys the written words, a sharp counter-scene to that assurance.

basis: royal burning of the scroll
note: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the written columns; its deliberate loss gives a concrete contrary case to the commentary's claim that divine collection is not dropped.

basis: rewrite the burned scroll's former words
note: After the scroll is burned, YHWH commands another scroll containing the former words, making restoration after textual loss part of the parallel.

basis: rewritten scroll with additional words
note: After the scroll is burned, Jeremiah dictates again and Baruch writes a replacement with more words; this gives the commentary's movement from loss to recollection and pages a concrete recovery narrative.

basis: former scroll restored with additional words
note: After the burning, Baruch writes the former words from Jeremiah's mouth and many similar words are added; this distinct final step makes remembered speech both recoverable and expandable in a new scroll.

basis: Jeremiah dictates; Baruch writes
note: The commentary's reading-to-pages sequence is enacted when Jeremiah speaks God's words and Baruch writes them on a scroll.

basis: Baruch writes from Jeremiah's mouth
note: Baruch writes the divine words from Jeremiah's mouth on a scroll, a particularly close scene of mediated recital becoming pages.

basis: Job wishes his words written in a book
note: The commentary traces recitation into written pages; Job asks for his own words to be recorded in a book, a lament's appeal for durable preservation.

basis: Job desires his words inscribed permanently
note: Job's wish that his words be written in a book makes durable inscription the response to threatened loss in a non-prophetic setting, extending the commentary's concern with pages that hold what speech might otherwise lose.

basis: words engraved in rock with iron and lead
note: The commentary says the written pages preserve what memory might lose; Job intensifies the wish by asking for words cut permanently into rock.

basis: book in the mouth and day-night meditation
note: Joshua is told that the Torah book must not depart from his mouth and must be meditated on continually, combining a book, oral repetition, and obedient retention.

basis: Hebrew זכרון (zikaron, remembrance)
note: The commentary makes dhikr both preservation and remembrance; Malachi uses the cognate in a book written for those who fear the Lord and honor his name, joining remembered devotion to a written record.

basis: fearers, the Lord's name, book of remembrance
note: The commentary says the one who fears will remember and that remembrance of the Lord's name leads to prayer; Malachi's fearers honor the name and are recorded in a book of remembrance.

basis: book of remembrance for those who fear the Name
note: Those who fear YHWH are recorded in a book of remembrance before him, bringing together fear, the divine Name, remembering, and a written record as in 87:9-10 and 15-19.

basis: distinction between those serving God and those not
note: The commentary separates the one who fears and remembers from the one who avoids reminder; Malachi says a coming distinction will be made between the righteous and the wicked.

basis: remember the Torah of Moses
note: The closing command to remember Moses' Torah makes remembrance itself the mode by which a Mosaic written legacy remains operative.

basis: reading the Law with explanation so people understand
note: The commentary treats reminder as an aid to recover needed knowledge; Nehemiah describes public reading of the book with explanation that makes its meaning clear to listeners.

basis: Hebrew q-r-ʾ / Arabic q-r-ʾ
note: Hebrew q-r-ʾ is used for public reading of God's written Torah with explanation; its formal cognacy with the commentary's قرأ makes 87:6's recitation a textual and communal act, not only private memory.

basis: visible fringe as a reminder to obey
note: The tassel is to be seen so Israel remembers and performs the commands; it gives a material tadhkira-like aid to recall.

basis: do not forget teaching; let the heart keep commands
note: The commentary opposes forgetting to keeping entrusted teaching; Proverbs pairs an explicit command not to forget with the heart's custody of instruction.

basis: do not forget teaching; heart keeps commands
note: Forgetting Torah is opposed to the heart's keeping commandments, closely matching the commentary's definition of forgetting as failure to hold what was entrusted.

basis: teaching written on the heart
note: The commentary moves between memory and physical pages; Proverbs says to bind fidelity around the neck and write it on the heart, relocating inscription inside the learner.

basis: word stored in the heart to prevent sin
note: The commentary depicts teaching retained rather than lost; the psalmist says he has stored God's word in his heart so he will not sin.

basis: I will not forget your word
note: The psalmist's pledge not to forget God's word is the direct devotional counterpart to the commentary's contrast between forgetting and preserving.

basis: lost sheep; seek your servant; I have not forgotten
note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has gone missing; the psalmist asks God to seek him as a lost sheep while affirming that he remembers God's commandments.

basis: never forgetting precepts that preserve life
note: The commentary says remembrance is the opposite of forgetting and that remembered teaching is kept; the psalmist says God's precepts preserve life and therefore will not be forgotten.

basis: remember God's works and keep commandments
note: The commentary says remembrance preserves teaching; the psalm's intergenerational instruction aims to make children hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commands.

basis: the speakers deny return after death
note: The commentary affirms an afterlife better and more lasting than present life; Wisdom's speakers argue that death has no return, directly opposing that horizon.

basis: the speakers urge enjoyment of present goods
note: The commentary says people prefer present worldly life although the afterlife is more lasting; Wisdom's speakers instead propose enjoying the good things available now, voicing the contrary valuation.

basis: Moses' authorship and the catalog of biblical books
note: The rabbinic discussion that attributes Moses' book and other works to named authors is a later Jewish way of organizing the textual corpus behind the commentary's named Mosaic pages.

basis: Torah given scroll by scroll or as one whole
note: The rabbinic dispute over separate scrolls versus a completed Torah directly frames the commentary's progression from written sheets to a gathered codex as a question about revelation's material form.

basis: one hundred versus one hundred and one reviews
note: The contrast between reviewing a lesson one hundred and one times versus one hundred times supplies a rabbinic practice of repetition aimed at preventing the loss the commentary calls forgetting.

basis: Abraham fulfilled Torah before Sinai
note: By reading Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's observance of the whole Torah before its giving to Moses, the tradition supplies a Jewish bridge to 87:19's Abraham-and-Moses pairing.

basis: remember Sabbath over wine
note: The rabbinic derivation of Sabbath remembrance over wine interprets the Hebrew cognate z-k-r as enacted recall, sharpening the liturgical side of the commentary's ذ ك ر.
